one_liner: Rust DataFrame engine with lazy query optimization and SIMD execution; ~45x faster CSV writing than pandas.
what_it_does: Polars is a multi-threaded analytical query engine for DataFrames, written in Rust, with bindings for Python, Node.js, R, and SQL. It uses an expression-based API (`pl.col(...)`, lazy `.scan_parquet().filter().group_by().agg()`) rather than pandas' index-based `.loc`/`.iloc` model, so it is not a drop-in replacement. Data is held in the Apache Arrow columnar format for zero-copy interop, and a streaming engine can process datasets larger than available RAM.
how_it_is_fast: The core engine is multi-threaded and vectorized (SIMD) over Arrow's columnar memory layout, with a lazy execution mode whose query optimizer applies predicate/projection pushdown so only needed data is read and computed. The specific CSV-writer speedup (0.20.19 to 0.20.30) came from PR #15576, which replaced generic per-value serialization with a dedicated serializer per datatype, cutting function-call overhead and type conversions during writing.
when_to_use: Reading/writing large Parquet or CSV files (hundreds of MB to multi-GB) where pandas' single-threaded loops bottleneck
Datasets larger than RAM, using the streaming engine (`collect(engine='streaming')`)
Multi-core machines where a query (joins, group-by, filters) can be parallelized across threads and columns
Teams willing to adopt the expression/lazy API instead of pandas indexing semantics
Multi-language pipelines (Python/Rust/Node/R) that want to share Arrow memory zero-copy
when_not_to_use: Codebases tightly coupled to pandas' `.loc`/`.iloc`/index-based API - migrating is real engineering work, not a swap
Row counts above ~4.2 billion (2^32) - the default build uses 32-bit indexing and needs a bigidx build
Pre-2011 CPUs or CPUs without AVX2 - the default release build targets modern instruction sets; use the `LTS_CPU=1` build instead
x86-64 Python installs running under Rosetta on Apple Silicon need special install handling per the docs

Treating the 45x/3.5x numbers as proof of CSV *read* speed - this benchmark measures a Parquet-read + CSV-write pipeline on a first-party blog post with no published benchmark code or build flags, and pandas/pyarrow figures come from plots, not stated absolute times

integration.form: crate (Rust workspace of polars-* crates) + prebuilt Python wheel / Node package / R package
integration.dependencies: none required beyond the language runtime for prebuilt packages; internally vendors its own Arrow implementation (polars-arrow) rather than depending on the reference Arrow crate
integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2024 (recent rustc, e.g. 1.85+) for building from source; Python >=3.10 for py-polars
integration.platforms: x86-64 (AVX2 assumed by default release build; LTS_CPU=1 build for older CPUs), aarch64; optional NVIDIA GPU acceleration for query execution
integration.thread_safety: not documented beyond 'multi-threaded execution' internally; README does not state whether DataFrame/LazyFrame objects are safe to mutate concurrently from application code
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — expression-based lazy/eager API differs from pandas; not a drop-in for pandas.read_csv/to_csv call sites, requires code changes

gotchas: Default release binaries assume AVX2; pre-2011 CPUs need the separate LTS_CPU=1 build
Default build indexes rows with 32-bit integers, capping datasets at ~4.2 billion (2^32) rows without a bigidx build
Apple Silicon users running an x86-64 Python build under Rosetta need special installation handling (per the install guide)
The quoted 45x/3.5x figures come from a plot in a first-party blog post with no benchmark code or build flags published, and measure Parquet-read+CSV-write, not a pure CSV-read microbenchmark
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Most siblings in this category (xan, cisv, qsv, zsv, Sep, go-simdcsv, simd-csv, vroom, zsv-ruby) are single-purpose CSV parsers; DuckDB is the closest comparable full engine. Pick Polars when you need a full DataFrame/query engine (joins, group-by, lazy optimization, larger-than-RAM streaming) and are migrating off pandas, not just parsing CSV as fast as possible — for pure CSV-read throughput, a dedicated parser like zsv/qsv/DuckDB is the better-evidenced choice since this benchmark only covers Polars' CSV write path.
verified_claims_summary: An official Polars blog post benchmarked reading 15 Parquet files (~800MB, NYC Yellow Tripdata) and writing the result to CSV on a MacBook Pro M3 (24GB RAM): Polars 0.20.30 is reported ~45x faster than pandas and ~3.5x faster than pyarrow on the CSV write step (ratios read from plots, no absolute pandas/pyarrow times or benchmark code given), and 0.20.30 itself is ~40% faster than 0.20.19 (8.975s vs 14.684s) due to PR #15576's per-datatype serializer.
status_note: Actively maintained — pushed to today, 39,859 stars, ~2,930 open issues on a large fast-moving repo; MIT-licensed and installable via `pip install polars` / `cargo add polars`, so vendoring is unnecessary.
sources_read: https://github.com/pola-rs/polars (issue search: performance regressions, thread-safety/panic/leak reports)
